content: Health organizations universally recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of an infant's life. However, in many countries, it is common to introduce additional fluids or foods before this period. Recent research has suggested that introducing solid foods around four months of age, while continuing to breastfeed, may offer greater protection against food allergies compared to exclusive breastfeeding for six months. Other studies have indicated that the risks associated with non-exclusive breastfeeding depend on the type of additional food or fluid provided. Given these findings, it was deemed necessary to update the previous review to include the latest evidence comparing exclusive breastfeeding with non-exclusive breastfeeding. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of introducing additional food or fluids to full-term, healthy breastfeeding infants, as well as to examine the timing and type of supplementation. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and relevant reference lists up to March 1, 2016. They included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving infants under six months of age that compared exclusive breastfeeding with breastfeeding supplemented by additional food or fluids. The review included 11 trials involving 2,542 infants and mothers, with nine trials (2,226 participants) providing data relevant to the outcomes of interest. Due to variations in outcome measures and time points, pooling results from the trials was challenging. Meta-analyses were only possible for two outcomes: breastfeeding duration (primary outcome) and weight change (secondary outcome). None of the trials reported on physiological jaundice, and infant mortality was reported in only one trial. Many older trials lacked sufficient methodological detail to assess the risk of bias, and most studies showed a high risk of other biases, with over half demonstrating a high risk of selection bias. The findings revealed that providing breastfeeding infants with artificial milk, compared to exclusive breastfeeding, did not significantly affect breastfeeding rates at hospital discharge (risk ratio [RR] 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.97 to 1.08; one trial, 100 infants; low-quality evidence). At three months, infants who received artificial milk had higher rates of any breastfeeding compared to exclusively breastfed infants (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.41; two trials, 137 infants; low-quality evidence). Infants given artificial milk in the first few days after birth exhibited fewer obvious or probable symptoms of allergy compared to exclusively breastfed infants (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.91; one trial, 207 infants; very low-quality evidence). Maternal confidence did not differ significantly between mothers of non-exclusively breastfed infants and those of exclusively breastfed infants (mean difference [MD] 0.10, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.54; one study, 39 infants; low-quality evidence). Breastfeeding rates were lower in the non-exclusive breastfeeding group compared to the exclusive breastfeeding group at four, eight, and 12 weeks (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.87; one trial, 170 infants; low-quality evidence), as well as at 16 and 20 weeks. The addition of glucose water reduced episodes of hypoglycemia (blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L) at 12 hours compared to exclusive breastfeeding (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.20; one trial, 170 infants; very low-quality evidence), but no significant difference was observed at 24 hours (RR 1.57, 95% CI 0.27 to 9.17; one trial, 170 infants; very low-quality evidence). Infants who received additional glucose water experienced less weight loss at six, 12, 24, and 48 hours of life (MD -32.50 g, 95% CI -52.09 to -12.91; low-quality evidence) compared to exclusively breastfed infants, but no difference was observed at 72 hours (MD 3.00 g, 95% CI -20.83 to 26.83; very low-quality evidence). In another trial combining water and glucose water groups (one trial, 47 infants), no significant difference in weight loss was found between the additional fluid group and the exclusively breastfed group on day three (MD -1.03%, 95% CI -2.24 to 0.18; very low-quality evidence) or day five (MD -0.20%, 95% CI -0.86 to 0.46; very low-quality evidence). Infant mortality was reported in one trial, with no deaths occurring in either group (1,162 infants). The early introduction of potentially allergenic foods, compared to exclusive breastfeeding, did not reduce the risk of food allergies to one or more of these foods between one and three years of age (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.25; 1,162 children), visible eczema at 12 months (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.44; 284 children), or food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome reactions (RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.18 to 22.04; 1,303 children) (all moderate-quality evidence). Breastfeeding infants who received additional foods from four months onward showed no significant difference in weight gain between 16 and 26 weeks compared to exclusively breastfed infants (MD -39.48 g, 95% CI -128.43 to 49.48; two trials, 260 children; low-quality evidence) or weight z-scores (MD -0.01, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.13; one trial, 100 children; moderate-quality evidence). In conclusion, the review found no evidence to suggest that the brief use of additional water or glucose water benefits newborns in terms of breastfeeding duration. The evidence on formula supplementation was insufficient to recommend a change in current practices favoring exclusive breastfeeding. For infants aged four to six months, no benefits or risks were identified regarding morbidity or weight change with the introduction of additional foods. The majority of studies were of low quality, with high risks of bias, limiting the ability to fully assess the benefits or harms of supplementation or the impact of its timing and type. The findings support the current international recommendation that healthy infants should be exclusively breastfed for the first six months of life.
